claims.text: Adding approximately 2–5 wt% tungsten during synthesis will promote in-situ formation of tungsten precipitates.
The tungsten precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly dispersed within the high-entropy-alloy matrix.
The tungsten precipitates will form continuous, percolative, high-conductivity paths.
These paths will improve phonon and electron transport.
Improved phonon and electron transport will increase the alloy's effective thermal conductivity.
A low volume fraction and fine dispersion of tungsten precipitates will preserve grain-boundary strengthening.
The tungsten modification will preserve overall mechanical integrity.
The tungsten-modified alloy will have an approximately 20–30% higher effective thermal conductivity than the unmodified alloy.
The tungsten-modified alloy will not undergo significant degradation in yield strength.
The tungsten-modified alloy will not undergo significant degradation in fracture toughness.
The proposed benefits will hold between 600°C and 900°C under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading representative of plasma-facing reactor operation.
The proposed benefits may cease above 900°C because phase stability or precipitate morphology could be compromised.
Extreme irradiation may compromise phase stability or precipitate morphology and invalidate the proposed benefits.

contradictions.description: The mediator is described as a low-volume-fraction, uniformly nano-dispersed precipitate population, while the mechanism requires those precipitates to form a continuous percolative network. The hypothesis does not explain how isolated nanoscale precipitates at only 2–5 wt% tungsten would also constitute continuous paths.
